prompt_free_text:
This paper addresses an important and timely topic: understanding what drives zero-shot cross-lingual transfer in multilingual language models. The central contribution is a narrative review that organizes prior work into five factor categories—linguistic similarity, lexical overlap, model architecture, pre-training settings, and pre-training data—and attempts not only to summarize findings but also to reconcile apparent contradictions across studies. This is a worthwhile goal. The multilingual NLP literature has indeed accumulated many partially overlapping empirical claims, often under different experimental setups, and a synthesis focused specifically on explanatory factors for transfer would be useful to the community.

The paper’s main strength is its clear motivation and reasonably coherent high-level taxonomy. The five-factor structure is intuitive and covers much of the literature that practitioners and researchers would naturally consult when asking why transfer works better for some language pairs, tasks, and models than others. I also appreciate that the authors do not merely list papers, but try to compare them and explain disagreements through differences in setup, such as synthetic versus natural languages, task type, model family, and feature-importance methodology. The sections on lexical overlap and syntax are especially useful in this regard: the paper makes a plausible case that some contradictions in the literature may be due to interactions between overlap and word order, or due to unrealistic perturbations such as random permutation being treated as “syntax change.” The discussion section also appropriately emphasizes interactions among factors and task-specific effects rather than presenting any single factor as universally dominant.

That said, in its current form, the paper falls short of the rigor I would expect from a top-tier review paper. The biggest issue is methodological. The paper presents itself as a review that identifies consensus and resolves conflicts, but it does not describe a systematic review protocol in enough detail to support strong claims of comprehensiveness or objectivity. There is no clear description of search strategy, inclusion and exclusion criteria, time window, venues searched, keywords used, screening process, or how papers were categorized. Appendix A lists surveyed papers, but this is not a substitute for a reproducible methodology. As a result, it is difficult to assess whether the literature coverage is balanced, whether important studies are missing, or whether the conclusions are influenced by selective inclusion. For a survey/review paper whose main contribution is synthesis, this is a substantial weakness.

Relatedly, many of the paper’s “resolution” claims are suggestive rather than firmly established. In several places, the authors propose explanations for contradictory findings, but these explanations are speculative and not always clearly distinguished from evidence-backed conclusions. For example, the discussion of why Ahuja et al. differs from Lin et al. and Srinivasan et al. on task-specific importance of lexical overlap hinges on the difference between Lasso and tree-based models. This is plausible, but the review does not provide enough comparative evidence to justify it as more than a hypothesis. Similarly, the claim that syntax may be overestimated because random permutation and inversion are unnatural perturbations is sensible, but the paper should more carefully separate “our interpretation” from “established consensus.” A review can and should offer synthesis, but it needs to signal confidence levels more explicitly.

A second major concern is that the taxonomy, while useful, sometimes blurs distinctions between correlated factors and causal mechanisms. Linguistic similarity, lexical overlap, writing system, tokenizer quality, vocabulary sharing, and pre-training corpus composition are deeply entangled. The paper acknowledges this, but the organization still tends to discuss them as separable dimensions more than the evidence warrants. For instance, lexical overlap is partly a function of script, tokenization, and vocabulary construction; “linguistic similarity” metrics such as WALS/lang2vec aggregate heterogeneous properties, some of which may correlate with geography or genealogy rather than directly affecting model behavior; and pre-training data source effects may be confounded with domain match to downstream evaluation. The review would be stronger if it more explicitly framed these categories as observational lenses rather than independent causal factors, and if it included a summary figure or conceptual model showing likely dependencies and confounds.

The coverage is generally solid for encoder-style multilingual models such as mBERT and XLM-R, but it feels somewhat narrow relative to the title’s broad promise of “multilingual language models.” In practice, the review is mostly about zero-shot transfer in masked language models and bilingual/small synthetic setups. The paper briefly notes in the discussion that generative models remain underexplored, but this limitation is more central than the current framing suggests. If the scope is really encoder-based MLLMs for discriminative zero-shot transfer, the title and framing should say so more explicitly. Otherwise, readers may expect broader coverage of multilingual seq2seq models, instruction-tuned multilingual LLMs, retrieval-augmented settings, or transfer in generation tasks.

I also found that some sections overstate the degree of consensus. For example, the paper says syntax has been “confirmed” as beneficial across many tasks, but the underlying evidence spans very different operationalizations of syntax, different tasks, and both natural and synthetic languages. Likewise, statements such as “target language pre-training corpus size and comparable corpora sources across languages have been identified as two crucial factors” are directionally reasonable, but “crucial” sounds stronger than the evidence summarized. A more calibrated style would improve the paper’s credibility: e.g., “frequently associated with,” “supported in several studies,” or “appears especially important under X conditions.”

Another weakness is that the review does not sufficiently evaluate the quality of the underlying evidence. Not all cited studies should carry equal weight: some are controlled synthetic experiments, some are correlational analyses over natural languages, some rely on feature importance from predictive meta-models, and some are based on a small number of language pairs or tasks. These designs answer different questions and have different inferential strengths. The paper often juxtaposes them productively, but it rarely makes explicit which kinds of evidence are stronger for causal claims and which are mainly descriptive. A stronger review would include a more systematic assessment of evidence types, perhaps distinguishing controlled intervention studies, observational correlational studies, and meta-prediction studies, and then temper conclusions accordingly.

The paper would also benefit from more precise treatment of evaluation settings. “Cross-lingual transfer” is used broadly, but transfer behavior differs substantially across token-level tasks, sentence-level classification, structured prediction, retrieval, and QA. The review mentions task-specific differences, but these are not synthesized into a clear framework. Similarly, source-language choice, target-language resource level, script overlap, and domain match are all likely moderators. A concise summary table of “what seems to matter most for which task families and under which conditions” would make the review much more actionable.

On presentation, the paper is generally readable, but there are several stylistic and editorial issues. Some claims are repetitive across sections. There are occasional grammatical problems and awkward phrasing, and a few sentences are too long or imprecise. The manuscript would benefit from careful copy-editing. I also noticed some formatting artifacts and footnote presentation issues in the provided text. These are minor compared with the conceptual concerns, but for a review paper, polish matters because clarity is part of the contribution.

I have a few more specific comments that could strengthen the paper substantially. First, the authors should add a dedicated methodology section describing how the literature was collected and screened. Even a lightweight systematic-review protocol would help. Second, the paper should explicitly define what it means by “resolve conflicts.” In many cases the paper offers hypotheses for reconciliation, not definitive resolution. Third, the authors should consider adding a summary matrix that maps factors to task types, evidence strength, and confidence level. Fourth, the review should more clearly distinguish between findings from natural-language studies and synthetic-language interventions, since these support different kinds of conclusions. Fifth, the discussion of feature-importance-based studies should include a caution that feature importance is model-dependent and unstable under correlated predictors; this is especially relevant given the paper’s reliance on such studies to infer factor salience. Sixth, the scope should be tightened or retitled to reflect that the review is primarily about encoder-based zero-shot transfer rather than multilingual language models in the broad contemporary sense.

I also think the paper misses an opportunity to articulate a sharper conceptual takeaway. Right now, the conclusion is essentially that many factors matter, interactions matter, and task-specific effects matter. That is true, but somewhat diffuse. Based on the surveyed evidence, the authors could propose a more explicit hierarchy such as: transfer depends on representational alignment emerging from shared parameter pressure and multilingual exposure; this alignment is facilitated by structural and lexical proximity, good tokenization, sufficient target-language pre-training data, and domain comparability; and the relative importance of these conditions varies by task granularity. A synthesis at that level would make the review more memorable and more useful.

Overall, I view the paper as a promising and potentially useful survey, but not yet at the level of rigor and synthesis expected for a top conference review paper. Its topic is important, the organization is sensible, and several of the cross-paper comparisons are insightful. However, the lack of a reproducible review methodology, the occasional overstatement of conclusions, and the insufficient separation of evidence from speculation limit its current contribution.

My recommendation is weak reject in its current form, with a clear path to improvement. If the authors strengthen the review methodology, calibrate claims more carefully, explicitly assess evidence quality, and sharpen the synthesis beyond a descriptive catalog of factors, this could become a valuable reference for the multilingual NLP community.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper is a narrative review of literature on zero-shot cross-lingual transfer in multilingual language models, aiming to unify explanations for why transfer emerges and what factors influence it. The authors organize prior work into five categories: linguistic similarity, lexical overlap, model architecture, pre-training settings, and pre-training data. For each category, they summarize empirical findings, discuss apparent contradictions across studies, and propose qualitative resolutions, often emphasizing interactions among factors and task-specific effects. The paper’s main contribution is a structured synthesis of prior studies rather than new experiments or formal theory.
strengths: Timely and relevant topic: understanding cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LMs is important for both scientific understanding and practical deployment, especially for low-resource languages.
Clear organizational structure around five factor categories, which makes the literature easier to navigate and provides a useful taxonomy for future work.
Broad coverage of prior work spanning linguistic, architectural, and data-centric explanations rather than focusing narrowly on one perspective.
The paper does more than list papers; it attempts to reconcile conflicting findings and highlights possible moderators such as task type, word order, script, and corpus size.

Useful discussion of limitations in the surveyed literature, including heterogeneity of methodologies, synthetic vs. natural language settings, and the risks of overinterpreting feature importance from predictive meta-models.
The review identifies several actionable research directions, including studying factor interactions, expanding multilingual evaluation datasets, and extending analysis to generative models.
weaknesses: The review is largely narrative and qualitative; it lacks a systematic review protocol, explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria, search strategy, or reproducible methodology for paper selection, which weakens claims of comprehensiveness and objectivity.

Many conclusions are stated with stronger certainty than the underlying evidence supports, especially when based on heterogeneous studies with different tasks, models, languages, and evaluation setups.

Several proposed resolutions of contradictory findings are speculative rather than empirically validated within the review itself; they are plausible hypotheses but are sometimes presented close to conclusions.

The paper does not provide a rigorous comparative framework for weighing evidence quality across studies (e.g., controlled synthetic studies vs. ecological natural-language studies, sample sizes, statistical significance, confound controls).

There is no quantitative synthesis or meta-analysis, even for recurring claims such as the role of syntax, lexical overlap, or corpus size; as a result, the review cannot estimate effect sizes or robustness.

Coverage appears somewhat uneven: linguistic similarity and lexical overlap receive detailed treatment, while model architecture and pre-training settings are discussed more briefly and with fewer critical caveats.

Some recommendations and hypotheses (e.g., organizing multilingual modeling around linguistic features rather than languages) are interesting but underdeveloped and not strongly grounded by the surveyed evidence.
methodological_flaws: The paper’s central claim of identifying 'consensuses' and resolving conflicts is not backed by a systematic evidence aggregation method. Without a formal review protocol or weighting scheme, the synthesis risks selection bias and subjective interpretation.

The review frequently infers causal explanations from correlational findings reported in prior work. For example, correlations between linguistic similarity or lexical overlap and transfer performance are sometimes discussed as explanatory mechanisms without sufficient separation from confounds such as script, domain, tokenizer quality, or pre-training data size.

Some conflict-resolution arguments rely on post hoc reasoning. For instance, explanations that lexical overlap matters mainly under dissimilar word order, or that discrepancies arise from linear vs. nonlinear predictive models, are plausible but not demonstrated by direct comparative evidence within the review.

The paper sometimes overgeneralizes from synthetic-language experiments to natural-language behavior while simultaneously acknowledging that synthetic languages may not capture real-world complexity. This tension is not resolved methodologically.

Feature-importance results from predictive models are discussed as evidence about underlying causal factors, despite the authors noting that such interpretations are not absolute. This creates inconsistency in scientific logic: the review critiques these methods yet still uses them substantively in several conclusions.

No formal assessment of empirical validity across cited studies is provided: there is little discussion of statistical uncertainty, reproducibility, benchmark overlap, publication bias severity, or whether reported effects hold across comparable evaluation settings.

The review does not clearly distinguish evidence about transfer performance from evidence about representation alignment or multilinguality more broadly; these are related but not identical constructs, and conflating them can weaken the logical precision of the synthesis.
